cards.q: Why must you run `sort` before `uniq -c` when counting how often each value appears?
cards.a: `uniq` only merges identical lines that sit next to each other. On unsorted input the same value gets several separate counts. The classic frequency count is `cut -d, -f2 file | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`.

cards.q: What does `chmod 750 run.sh` set, and how do you read the three digits?
cards.a: Read is 4, write is 2, execute is 1, added up per class. Owner 7 is rwx, group 5 is r-x, others 0 is nothing. The listing shows `-rwxr-x---`. For comparison, `-rw-r-----` is 640.

cards.q: What does `echo "n=$((7/2))"` print in bash, and what do you use when you need decimals?
cards.a: It prints `n=3`: bash arithmetic is integer-only and truncates. For decimals use `awk` or `bc`; for example `awk 'BEGIN{print 7/2}'` prints 3.5.

cards.q: Why does `[ $name = x ]` break when name is empty, and what is the safe form?
cards.a: Unquoted, an empty name disappears and the test becomes `[ = x ]`, a syntax error. Write `[ "$name" = x ]`. Spaces are required inside `[ ]`, and none are allowed around `=` in an assignment.

cards.q: A bad commit reached `main` three hours ago and four colleagues pulled it. Do you use `git revert` or `git reset --hard`?
cards.a: `git revert <hash>`, then push. It adds a new commit that undoes the change, so history is not rewritten and everyone just pulls one extra commit. Use `reset --hard` only on local commits nobody has pulled.

cards.q: After a rebase, why is a plain `git push --force` dangerous on a shared branch? What is the safer flag?
cards.a: Rebase gives your commits new hashes, so teammates' copies diverge and a force push can erase their work. Rebase only private branches. If you must force, use `--force-with-lease`; it refuses when someone else has pushed.

cards.q: How many usable host addresses does a /24 have? Give the general formula.
cards.a: 254. The formula is 2^(32 - prefix) - 2, because the network and broadcast addresses are reserved. A /23 gives 510. Some clouds reserve 5 addresses per subnet, so check their rule.

cards.q: RTT is 100 ms. How long until the first byte of an HTTPS (TLS 1.3) answer on a new connection, and on a reused one?
cards.a: About 300 ms on a new connection: TCP handshake (1 RTT), TLS 1.3 handshake (1 RTT), then request and response (1 RTT). A reused connection needs only the last step: 100 ms.

cards.q: Why does `counter += 1` in several threads lose updates, and how do you fix it?
cards.a: It is three steps: read, add, write. Two threads can read the same value, so one update is lost (a race). Wrap the whole read-modify-write in `with lock:`. A test that passes once proves nothing.

cards.q: A container with a 512 MiB limit exits with code 137. What happened?
cards.a: 137 = 128 + 9, so the process received SIGKILL. The kernel OOM killer ended it for exceeding its memory limit. Fix the leak or the limit, and size heaps from the cgroup limit, not from the host's RAM.

cards.q: What is the difference between HTTP 401 and 403?
cards.a: 401: the server does not know who you are (authentication missing or failed). 403: it knows you, but you may not do this (authorization failed). The fixes differ: log in versus change permissions.

cards.q: Why store passwords as slow salted hashes (bcrypt, PBKDF2, Argon2) rather than plain SHA-256 or encrypted text?
cards.a: A fast hash lets attackers test billions of guesses per second. A random salt per user stops shared hashes and lookup tables. Encryption is reversible, so one stolen key exposes everyone. A slow, salted, one-way hash limits the damage.

cards.q: A teammate pushed an API key to a public repo, then deleted the file in the next commit. Is it fixed?
cards.a: No. The key stays in Git history and forks, and scanners find it fast. Revoke and rotate the key first, then prevent a repeat with `.gitignore`, environment variables and a scanner such as gitleaks.

cards.q: Name three hidden loops that turn a loop body into O(n) work, making the whole loop O(n²).
cards.a: `x in my_list` scans the list, `s = s + 'a'` copies the string, and `list.pop(0)` or `insert(0, x)` shifts every item. Use a set, `''.join(parts)` and `deque` instead.

cards.q: In open addressing, why can't you delete a key by just emptying its slot? What do you do instead?
cards.a: Lookups stop at the first empty slot, so any key that was probed past it becomes unreachable. Mark the slot as a tombstone (deleted, keep probing) and rebuild the table when tombstones pile up.

cards.q: A prefix-sum array P has n+1 entries with P[0] = 0. What is the sum of a[l..r]?
cards.a: P[r+1] - P[l]. Writing P[r] - P[l] is the classic off-by-one. Example: a = [3,1,4,1,5,9,2,6], indexes 2 to 5 give P[6] - P[2] = 23 - 4 = 19.

cards.q: With `while lo < hi` and `m = (lo + hi) // 2`, which updates are safe, and why is `lo = m` a bug?
cards.a: Use `hi = m` and `lo = m + 1`. With `lo = m`, when hi = lo + 1 then m equals lo, so lo never moves and the loop runs forever. Do not mix templates, and test with 1 and 2 items.

cards.q: Why is `list.pop(0)` a trap in queue code, and what do you use instead?
cards.a: It shifts every remaining item left, so each pop is O(n) and a queue loop becomes O(n²). Use `collections.deque` with `append` and `popleft`, both O(1).

cards.q: To keep the K largest items of a huge stream, which heap do you keep, and what do time and memory cost?
cards.a: A min-heap of size K. Its root is the smallest of your current top K, so it is the one to evict when a larger item arrives. Time O(n log K), memory O(K).

cards.q: In BFS, why mark a node as seen when you push it, not when you pop it?
cards.a: If you mark on pop, the same node can be queued many times before it is popped, wasting time and memory. Marking on push puts each node in the queue once and keeps BFS at O(V + E).

cards.q: Why is checking only each node against its direct children not enough to validate a BST?
cards.a: A bad value deeper down slips through: a 9 inside the left subtree of 8 still passes its parent's check. Pass the allowed range (lo, hi) down the recursion and test every node against it.

cards.q: How does Kahn's topological sort detect a cycle?
cards.a: It repeatedly removes nodes with in-degree 0. If fewer nodes come out than the graph has, the leftovers form a cycle (a circular dependency). Fail loudly instead of returning a partial order.

cards.q: Why does greedy fail for coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6? What do you use instead?
cards.a: Greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins), but 3 + 3 uses only 2. Greedy is right only when the local best choice is provably safe. Use DP: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]) over the coins.

cards.q: `fib(20)` makes 21,891 calls without memoization. Why does a cache fix that, and when does it apply?
cards.a: The plain version recomputes the same sub-problems, so calls grow like 2ⁿ. With a cache each n is computed once: O(n). It needs overlapping sub-problems and an answer that depends only on the inputs.

cards.q: Coins 1, 2, 5 and amount 5: why do combinations (4) and ordered sequences (9) need different loop orders?
cards.a: Combinations: coins in the outer loop, amounts inside, so each coin set is counted once. Ordered sequences: amounts outside, coins inside. If your 'combinations' answer is 9, the loops are swapped.

cards.q: A cache of 4 nodes uses `hash mod N`. You add a fifth node. What fraction of keys stays put?
cards.a: Only 4/20 = 20% stay, so 80% move. Consistent hashing moves only the keys the new node takes over, about 1/5 of them, so the cache stays mostly warm.

cards.q: A service fails 30% of calls and each request is tried up to 3 times. How many calls reach the server per request, on average?
cards.a: 1 + 0.3 + 0.3² = 1.39, a 39% load increase. A request eventually succeeds with probability 1 - 0.3³ = 0.973. Retry only with backoff, jitter, a cap and idempotency keys.

cards.q: How much GPU memory do the weights of a 7B-parameter model need in float16 and in 4-bit? And training with Adam?
cards.a: float16 uses 2 bytes per parameter: 14 GB. 4-bit uses 0.5 byte: 3.5 GB. Training with Adam needs about 16 bytes per parameter before activations: 112 GB. Inference also needs a KV cache.

cards.q: What is arithmetic intensity, and how does it tell you whether work is memory-bound or compute-bound?
cards.a: FLOPs per byte moved. Compare it with the ridge point, peak FLOPS divided by bandwidth (100 TFLOPS / 1 TB/s = 100). Below it you are memory-bound (x + x: 0.083). Above it, compute-bound (3000 x 3000 matmul: 500).

cards.q: In Two Sum, why do you check the dictionary before storing the current number?
cards.a: Storing first lets an element pair with itself. For [3, 3] with target 6, storing first matches the first 3 with itself and returns (0, 0) instead of (0, 1). Check for the complement, then store.

quiz.q: Which command deletes every `*.tmp` file under the current folder, even when a file name contains a space?
quiz.why: `-print0` ends each name with a NUL byte and `xargs -0` splits on it, so spaces stay inside the name. The other three split names at spaces: in a test the plain pipe left `my file.tmp` in place and tried to remove `./my` and `file.tmp`.

quiz.q: What does `bash -c 'set -e; false || echo ignored; echo next'` print?
opts: Nothing: set -e stops the script at `false`
quiz.why: `set -e` does not fire for a command on the left side of `||` or `&&`, because its failure is being tested. So `echo ignored` runs and the script continues to `echo next`. Check steps that must not fail with an explicit test.

quiz.q: `main` has commits A-B-C. You branched from B and made D. You merge your branch into `main`. What does Git create?
opts: A fast-forward: main simply moves to D
A rebase that replays D on top of C
Nothing: Git refuses until you rebase
A merge commit with parents C and D
quiz.why: A fast-forward is only possible when main has no new commits. Here main moved on to C, so the histories diverged and Git creates a merge commit with two parents. Merge never replays commits the way a rebase does.

quiz.q: A page makes 12 sequential API calls. Each has RTT 40 ms and 10 ms of server time. What is the minimum total time?
quiz.why: Each call costs 40 + 10 = 50 ms and they run one after another: 12 x 50 = 600 ms. 480 forgets the server time. Running the calls in parallel would take about 50 ms, which is why batching beats buying bandwidth.

quiz.q: You must speed up four CPU-heavy pure-Python tasks on a 12-core machine. Which choice helps most?
quiz.why: The GIL lets one thread run Python bytecode at a time, so threads and asyncio give about the serial time for CPU-bound work. Separate processes have their own interpreters and can use separate cores. Threads and asyncio shine when tasks mostly wait.

quiz.q: A users table has 3 rows and the input is `x' OR '1'='1`. How many rows come back from an f-string query `WHERE name='{name}'` and from a parameterized `WHERE name=?`?
quiz.why: The f-string closes the quote early and appends `OR '1'='1'`, which is true for every row, so all 3 rows leak. The parameterized query treats the whole string as one name that nobody has, so it returns 0 rows.

quiz.q: An attacker edits an HS256 JWT's payload to `role: admin` and keeps the old signature. What happens at the server?
opts: It is rejected, because the signature no longer matches the payload
It is accepted: the server only checks that the token has three parts
It is accepted if the token has not expired
The edit is impossible, because JWT payloads are encrypted
quiz.why: The signature is an HMAC over header and payload with the server's secret. A changed payload no longer matches it. The payload is only base64url encoded, so anyone can read and edit it, but nobody can forge a valid signature without the key.

quiz.q: A 7-slot table uses h(k) = k mod 7 with linear probing. You insert 15, 22, 8, 1 in that order. In which slot does 1 land?
quiz.why: All four keys hash to slot 1. 15 takes slot 1, 22 probes on to slot 2, 8 to slot 3, and 1 tries slots 1, 2 and 3 before finding slot 4 free. Slot 1 is only its home slot.

quiz.q: What is the largest sum of a contiguous subarray of `[-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]`?
quiz.why: Kadane's rule is cur = max(x, cur + x). The best run is 4, -1, 2, 1 = 6. Extending it by -5 and 4 gives only 5. 4 is just the largest single item, and 12 adds all positives although they are not contiguous.

quiz.q: What does `import heapq; h = [9, 4, 7, 1, 6, 2]; heapq.heapify(h); print(h)` print?
quiz.why: `heapify` only makes every parent at most its children, so the list is not sorted. Only `h[0]` is guaranteed to be the minimum. Sorted order needs repeated `heappop` calls.

quiz.q: You need shortest paths from one source in a graph that has negative edge weights but no negative cycle. Which algorithm fits?
quiz.why: Dijkstra assumes non-negative weights because it finalises a node when popped. BFS counts hops, not weights. Kruskal builds a spanning tree, a different problem. Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V - 1 times and can detect negative cycles.

quiz.q: Edges: 0-1, 0-2, 1-3, 1-4, 2-4, 2-5, 4-6, 5-7, 6-7. How many shortest paths go from node 0 to node 6?
quiz.why: BFS layers: {0}, {1, 2}, {3, 4, 5}, {6, 7}. Node 6 is reached only through 4, and 4 has two parents in the previous layer (1 and 2). The paths are 0-1-4-6 and 0-2-4-6. The route through 7 is longer.

quiz.q: A subsets function appends `cur` (not `cur[:]`) to `res`, using `cur.append(x)`, recursion, then `cur.pop()`. For `[1, 2]`, what is `res` at the end?
quiz.why: `res` holds four references to the same list `cur`. After all the pops `cur` is empty, so every entry shows []. Saving `cur[:]` stores a snapshot copy of each subset instead.

quiz.q: One item (weight 3, value 4), capacity 7. A buggy 0/1 knapsack loops capacities upward. What is `dp[7]` at the end?
quiz.why: Looping upward lets dp[6] = dp[3] + 4 and dp[7] = dp[4] + 4 reuse the item, so it is counted twice for 8. That is the unbounded knapsack. The true 0/1 answer is 4, which a downward loop gives.

quiz.q: A 5-node Raft cluster splits into groups of 3 and 2. Which statement is correct?
opts: Both groups elect a leader and keep accepting writes
Neither group can work, because the cluster is split
Only the group of 3 can elect a leader and commit writes
The group of 2 keeps writing if it still has the old leader
quiz.why: Committing needs a majority: 3 of 5. Two majorities of 5 always share a node, so two leaders cannot both commit. The group of 2 may still hold the old leader, but it can never reach a majority.

quiz.q: N = 3 replicas. Which read and write quorum does NOT guarantee that a read overlaps the latest write?
quiz.why: The rule is W + R > N. Here 1 + 2 = 3 is not greater than 3, so a read can miss the one node that took the write. The others sum to 4. Note that W = 1, R = 3 is fresh but reads fail if any node is down.

quiz.q: A team sizes a 13-billion-parameter float16 model as '13 GB' and buys a 16 GB GPU. What went wrong?
opts: Nothing: 13 GB fits with 3 GB to spare
float16 needs 2 bytes per parameter, so the weights alone are 26 GB
float16 needs 4 bytes per parameter, so the weights are 52 GB
The weights are 13 GB but the optimizer adds 16 bytes per parameter for inference
quiz.why: Memory = parameters x bytes per parameter. float16 is 2 bytes: 13e9 x 2 = 26 GB, before the KV cache. In 4-bit it would be 6.5 GB. Four bytes per parameter is float32, which would give 52 GB.

quiz.q: An LRU cache of capacity 2 runs put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3), get(2), put(4,4), get(1), get(3), get(4). What do the five get calls return, in order?
quiz.why: get(1) refreshes key 1, so put(3,3) evicts key 2 and get(2) is -1. Then put(4,4) evicts key 1, the least recently used, so get(1) is -1, while 3 and 4 are still cached.
